questions.prompt: Explain the differences between the is, as?, and as! operators in Swift.

rubric.criterion: Explains that is tests whether an instance matches a type and returns a boolean
Explains that as? conditionally downcasts and returns an optional (nil on failure)
Explains that as! force-downcasts and crashes at runtime if the cast fails

questions.modelAnswer: The is operator checks whether an instance is of a specific type and returns a boolean (true or false). The as? operator conditionally downcasts to a type, returning an optional that contains the value on success or nil on failure. The as! operator force-downcasts and triggers a runtime crash if the cast fails.

questions.prompt: Compare Any and AnyObject in Swift, explaining what kinds of values each can hold.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Any can represent any type at all, including structs, enums, functions, and classes
Explains that AnyObject can only represent instances of class types (reference types)

questions.modelAnswer: Any can represent an instance of any type in Swift, including value types like structs, enums, tuples, primitive numbers, and functions, as well as classes. AnyObject is restricted to reference types, meaning it can only represent instances of class types.

questions.prompt: Does type casting alter the underlying instance in memory, and how should downcasting be performed safely in production code?

rubric.criterion: States that type casting does not modify or reallocate the underlying instance in memory
Explains that safe downcasting in production uses as? paired with optional binding (if let or guard let)

questions.modelAnswer: Type casting does not modify, convert, or reallocate the underlying instance in memory. It only changes how the compiler treats the reference. In production code, downcasting should be performed safely using as? combined with optional binding (if let or guard let) to handle failures gracefully without crashes.

Explains that case is TargetType checks the type without binding a constant

questions.modelAnswer: In a switch statement, case let name as TargetType checks the item type. It binds the downcast value to a local constant. To verify the type without binding, case is TargetType tests the type and runs the branch directly.

questions.prompt: Why do senior Swift developers discourage storing collections of [Any] and recommend generics or protocols instead?

rubric.criterion: Explains that [Any] bypasses compile-time type safety and requires manual runtime downcasting
Explains that protocols and generics preserve static type safety and clarify API contracts

questions.modelAnswer: Storing collections of [Any] strips compile-time type safety, forcing callers to guess types and use runtime downcasts that can fail. Generics and protocols preserve static type checking, catch mismatched types during compilation, and clearly express expected capabilities in API contracts.
